We can use Gaussian elimination to find the general solutions of systems with any number of equations and variables. For instance, consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1, \\ y+3z &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This system has the augmented matrix
![](images/8a/8a8452587098eed9b697c3999c356359b949429f29ce16af2c81cf728be9480e.svg)

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\, & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+4z &=1 \\ y+3z &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We see that the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable $z.$ From the second equation, we get $y=-3z,$ and from the first equation, we obtain $x=1-4z.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1-4z, \\ y &=-3z, \\ z &=z.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1-4z \\ -3z \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+z\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

The augmented matrix for this system is
![](images/be/bed2784d17ee63b805917b492052daa7ef079c1682bbc78468eb10f314a92b1f.svg)

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 5 & 2 & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now
![](images/91/91175ab97472067cd14ffff740bb3a98718436f1e94de7a4a6d7fdfb1b35b81f.svg)

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $z,$ and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $z$ in terms of $y.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-1-5y \\ y &=y \\ z &=3,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1-5y \\ y \\ 3\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that a system of linear equations is called **consistent** if it has at least one solution. Otherwise, if there are no solutions, the system is called **inconsistent**. 

For a consistent system, 

- the system is called **consistent independent** if the solution is unique, while

- the system is called **consistent dependent** if there are infinitely many solutions.

![](images/f5/f5b808eac6e1d865b13b68ce2a4f7d317560ae3965928e478531fcd2148c2c6b.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & k & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & k+4 & -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

If $k=-4,$ then the second equation is $0=-5,$ which is false, and the system will have no solution.

Therefore, our system is inconsistent when $k=-4.$

To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is
![](images/3e/3e3e8adb0d6e13f7d3b4c3e450b25a789480ac53189ab92385174688e460b2cc.svg)

Using Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 4 \\ -4 & 6 & -8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now
![](images/41/4122fb4ef56aa99161b15bc25001ca728a6cf7dae36d5dac0aac9b03dc411685.svg)

Since any numbers $x$ and $y$ form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
2x -3y= 4
$$

The basic variable is $x,$ and we have a free variable $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$ 

Therefore, since there are infinitely many solutions, we conclude that the system is *consistent dependent*.

As a result, only statement I is true.

Consider a vector $\mathbf{u}$ which is given in terms of the vectors $\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\mathbf{v_2}$ as follows:

$$
{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}\mathbf{v_1}}+({\color{red}-2}){\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}} = \mathbf{u}
$$

Here, we say that $\mathbf{u}$ is a **linear combination** of the vectors ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v_1}}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}$ with coefficients ${\color{red}3}$ and ${\color{red}-2}$ respectively. 

In general, a linear combination of $n$ vectors $\mathbf{v_1},\mathbf{v_2},\dots,\mathbf{v_n}$ is the *weighted sum*

$$
{\color{red}x_1}\mathbf{\color{blue}v_1}+{\color{red}x_2}\mathbf{\color{blue}v_2}+\cdots + {\color{red}x_n}\mathbf{\color{blue}v_n} = \mathbf{u},
$$

where ${\color{red}x_1},{\color{red}x_2},\dots,{\color{red}x_n}\in\mathbb{R}.$ We say that $\mathbf{u}$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{\color{blue}v_1},\mathbf{\color{blue}v_2},\dots,\mathbf{\color{blue}v_n}$ with coefficients (or *weights*) ${\color{red}x_1},{\color{red}x_2},\dots,{\color{red}x_n},$ respectively.

For instance, 
![](images/ff/ff71636b9b5a34fec4de37b5e924c1c6bc3765c1ee823b325f5b0e01c0dc472a.svg)
is the linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{\color{blue}v_1},\mathbf{\color{blue}v_2},\mathbf{\color{blue}v_3}$ with coefficients ${\color{red}2}, {\color{red}0}, {\color{red}\dfrac{1}{2}},$ respectively.

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $q$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}+q{a}_{2} & =b \\ 2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+q[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}18 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ q[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}18 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ q[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}14 \\ 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

From the final equation above, we can tell that $q=2.$

{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 1 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

flags.detail: Literal brackets around a layout environment

value:
Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $t$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}+t{a}_{2} & =0 \\ 2[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ t[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 1 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\ t[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-16 \\ -2 \\ 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the first components, we get 

$$
-4t=-16\,⟹\,t=4.
$$

But then 

$$
\begin{aligned}4[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{aligned}]\ne [\begin{aligned}-16 \\ -2 \\ 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is no $t$ such that 
 $2{a}_{1}+t{a}_{2}=0.$

$$

Equating the first components, we get

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}\ne \begin{bmatrix}-16 \\ -2 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is no $t$ such that 
 $2{a}_{1}+t{a}_{2}=0.$

If $x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2\mathbf{a}_2 + x_3\mathbf{a}_3 = \mathbf b,$ then what is $x_1+x_2+x_3?$

value:
Since $\mathbf{b}$ is a linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{a_1}, \,\mathbf{a_2}$ and $\mathbf{a_3}$ with coefficients $x_1,\, x_2$ and $x_3,$ respectively, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3} & =b \\ {x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ -{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=7\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

![](images/9b/9bf913744317fab321cf9f2e01da732853a52a4fd7948c65da596ae4706f6dce.svg)

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{3} &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $x_3 = 2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_2 = -1,
$$

and substituting $x_3=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x_1+2(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_1 = -3.
$$

So the solution of the system is $x_1=-3, x_2=-1, x_3=2,$ which means

$$
-3 \mathbf{a_1}- \mathbf{a_2} +2 \mathbf{a_3}= \mathbf{b}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
x_1+x_2+x_3=-3-1+2=-2.
$$

Suppose that we want to know the values of $x$ and $y$ that satisfy *both* of the equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y &=-4 \\ 6x-y &=6.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We call this a **system of linear equations**. The equations of the system define two straight lines, so we can visualize the system by plotting both lines on the same graph.

![](images/59/59f16d57e74fd94fdab464eca22cea1271b19a3b78114446e31343cfabd15a12.png)

The solution of the system corresponds to the point where the two lines intersect. In this case, it is the point $(2,6)$, as shown above. So $x=2$ and $y=6$ form the **solution** to the system. We can write the solution as the ordered pair $(2, 6).$

Whenever we find a solution to a system of equations, it is a good idea to double-check our result. To check that the solution $x=2,y=6$ is the correct solution, we substitute our solution into *both* of the equations. 

Let's check the first equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & \,=\,-4 \\ (2)-(6) & =-4 \\ -4 & =-4\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now we check the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-y & \,=\,6 \\ 6(2)-6 & =6 \\ 6 & =6\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x=2$ and $y=6$ satisfied *both* equations, it is indeed the solution to the system of equations.

Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$
![](images/7c/7c2283c7de572acfc58b443499598554ecf3d26b1a13c48c80b8d6aadf7b576a.svg)

The matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form, but we can transform it even further into the **reduced row echelon form** (RREF) using the standard **Gauss-Jordan** method. 

The algorithm is similar to the algorithm of converting a matrix to row echelon form, except that we need to make *all* the pivot entries equal to $1$ and *all* the entries below *and above* a pivot (in a pivot column) equal to $0.$

In our case, we convert $M$ to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The final matrix is in reduced row echelon form:

- all the pivot entries are equal to $1$ (here we have $\color{red}1$'s on the main diagonal), and

Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$
![](images/7c/7c2283c7de572acfc58b443499598554ecf3d26b1a13c48c80b8d6aadf7b576a.svg)

The matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form, but we can transform it even further into the **reduced row echelon form** (RREF) using the standard **Gauss-Jordan** method. 

The algorithm is similar to the algorithm of converting a matrix to row echelon form, except that we need to make *all* the pivot entries equal to $1$ and *all* the entries below *and above* a pivot (in a pivot column) equal to $0.$

In our case, we convert $M$ to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The final matrix is in reduced row echelon form:

- all the pivot entries are equal to $1$ (here we have $\color{red}1$'s on the main diagonal), and

- all the entries below and above a pivot are equal to ${\color{blue}0}.$

1\. First, reduce the matrix to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination method (also making all pivot entries equal to $1$). 
  ![](images/5c/5c0f5ac3d95843b142c90e8ce83378ea2b2ad693baba6670e0cde46a449f5225.svg)

  - if $a_{23} \neq 0$, then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{23})R_3$, and

  - if $a_{13} \neq 0$, then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1 + (-a_{13})R_3$.

  - if $a_{12} \neq 0$, then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1 + (-a_{12})R_2$.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to reduced row echelon form.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$

$$

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x+2y &=16 \
	(4+y) + 2y &=16\
	4+3y &=16\
	3y &=12\

}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=4+y$, then we can find the value of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x &= 4 + y \
	   &= 4 + (4) \
	   &=8
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 8$ and $y = 4$, which can be written as $(8, 4).$

$$

If we now substitute $n=128$ into $y=64+17n$, then we can find the value of $y:$

$$

$$

Using the second equation, we can isolate $d$ adding to both sides of the equation $50t:$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:
![](images/77/77459b19bb1fd1f28e05e6f613e4e49af34595eae33eeeca584d65a289f7ea2c.svg)

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $u$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+6v-8 &= 0 \
2u+6v &= 8 \
2u &= 8 - 6v \
u &= \dfrac{8-6v}{2} \
u &= 4 - 3v
}
$$

Then, we substitute $u=4-3v$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $v\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \
	2(4-3v)+9v-6 &= 0 \
	8-6v+9v-6 &= 0 \
2+3v &= 0 \
3v &= -2 \
v &= -\dfrac{2}{3}
}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $u\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \
	2u+9\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) -6 &= 0 \
	2u-6-6 &= 0 \
	2u-12 &= 0 \
	2u &= 12 \
	u &= 6
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=6$ and $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, which can be written as $\left(6,-\dfrac{2}{3}\right).$

Let's consider a system of linear equations where the corresponding coefficient matrix is singular. For example, consider the following system and its associated augmented matrix:
![](images/6a/6a69daf7712312876b0ec97c540bbc472e46a7938beb8a59e694a04ad0b1d8c6.svg)

To solve the system, we can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as usual. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -5 \\ -3 & 6 & 15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now
![](images/a8/a8bfe3f6b27247ee9b27db8346fd94fb9068c85dec6f4a71517a821dee48dbf3.svg)

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 2y = -5.
$$

Finally, we describe the **general solution** of our system.

- The first variable in our equation, $x,$ is called a **basic variable**.

- The second variable in our equation, $y,$ is called a **free variable**.

Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x = -5+2y.$ So the general solution of the system is
![](images/0b/0ba4a232f29dd6fce2a8f6d7cda39b4f5b192c20fc91fe4403dfe648231382c5.svg)
where the free variable $y$ is any number.

In vector form, this solution is written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5+2y \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is the equation of a straight line on a plane. Any point on this line satisfies our system of equations.

If we want to find some **particular solution** of the system, we simply choose some particular value of $y$ and find the corresponding value of $x$ on the line. For example, if we choose $y=0,$ then the corresponding value is $x=-5$ and the particular solution is $x=-5,$ $y=0.$

Given a $2 \times 2$ system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:

- The system has exactly *one solution* if and only if the respective coefficient matrix is non-singular (meaning that the determinant is not zero). Such systems are called **consistent independent**.

- The system has *infinitely many solutions* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s. These systems are called **consistent dependent**.

- The system has *no solution* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s on the left-hand side and a non-zero element on the right-hand side. These are called **inconsistent** systems.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

**Note:** A system of linear equations of the form 
![](images/cb/cb397dd01794f28ff11c01079e287d63175e439c8bbaa85cd02dc61689780fa8.svg)
where we have only $0$'s on the right-hand side, is called **homogeneous**. A homogeneous system always has at least one solution, namely, the solution $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle 0,0 \rangle.$

Matrices arise naturally in *many* real-world problems. Weather forecasting, image processing and computer graphics, video games, and online customization algorithms are just a few of the many applications of matrices. Let's consider an example where we can use a matrix to model bus routes in a city. The diagram below shows the bus routes between three stations (Station A, Station B, and Station C) in a particular city, where $A, B,$ and $C$ represent the stations and the arrows represent the directed routes between them. ![](images/cb/cbdf5c2470229ae3ba10ee18bccd2dc764407897397466b157474bf2b819f5d9.png) Note that the circles $A,B,$ and $C$ in our diagram are called **nodes**. We wish to represent this same diagram using a matrix. Let's start by putting this information into a table like the one below:

Finally, keeping only the essential information, we obtain the following matrix: $$ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} $$

When we reduce a matrix to row echelon form, the number of *pivot* columns plus the number of *non-pivot* columns always equals the total number of columns of the matrix. 

By translating this into the language of vector spaces, we get the **rank-nullity theorem**. The rank-nullity theorem relates the rank of a matrix to the dimension of its null space:

*Let $A$ be a matrix (not necessarily square) with $n$ columns. Then,*

$$
\textrm{dim(Col}(A)) + \textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n),
$$

*or, equivalently,*

$$
\textrm{rank}(A) + \textrm{nullity}(A) = n.
$$

For example, suppose that for some matrix $A,$ we have

![](images/30/30f6472f02a4ac47f285fff05e0cdbf56367acdd18231271dc3dccf0040901bd.svg)

We can use the rank-nullity theorem to calculate $\textrm{rank}(A).$

In this case, we must have $n=4,$ since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space. 

Also, we must have $\textrm{nullity}(A)=2,$ since 
![](images/b5/b5f38590a71a2f8e1f29a5ba98920a10037737c1ebcbd3fd60f08a3e47555141.svg)

Therefore, using the rank-nullity theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+2 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

I. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the bottom of the matrix.

II. Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

$$

Let's consider our matrices $A$ and $B$ once more, with the leading entries highlighted.

![](images/af/af61f32297e248ab9989ba59ea6c9bda2f99efe19d25df525fef916617843a32.svg)

We say that a matrix is in **row echelon form** if it satisfies the following conditions:

I. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

II. Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

Here, $B$ is in row echelon form since both conditions are satisfied. However, $A$ is not in row echelon form since condition II is violated: the leading entry of the third row $(a_{32}={\color{red}1})$ is placed just below the leading entry of the second row $(a_{22}=3).$

Generally speaking, row echelon form means that we have *stairs* where each step (represented by a leading entry $\bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\large\ast}$) has a height of $1.$

![](images/67/67f83c454e59d16ae80cf67a19b19f968182251a2e5d1b405e2c422e0313d5b7.png)

Finally, an *augmented* matrix is in row echelon form if the coefficient matrix (i.e., the part that is to the left of the vertical bar) is in row echelon form.

Suppose we are given an $n \!\times\! n$ invertible matrix $A.$ Remember that if $A$ is invertible, then the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.$

Let's extract all possible information from this fact using the vector spaces related to the matrix, namely, the *column space* and the *null space*.

- The fact that the unique solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ is $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ tells us that 

$$
\textrm{Null}(A)=\{ \mathbf{0} \},
$$

 or alternatively, 

$$
\textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{nullity}(A)=0.
$$

- Furthermore, if $\textrm{dim(Null}(A))=0$ then $A$ has no *non-pivot* columns, or equivalently, all the columns of $A$ are *pivot columns*. So 

$$
\textrm{dim(Col}(A))=\textrm{rank}(A)=n.
$$

- Finally, since $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its basis has $n$ linearly independent vectors, we can conclude that 

$$
\textrm{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n.
$$

All the results mentioned above can be summarized in the following theorem, called the **invertible matrix theorem**:

*Let $A$ be an $n \!\times\! n$ matrix. Then we have the following equivalence:*
![](images/7e/7ef5d72a30dd7f79f6182c4d78d705a7771f9f90ff0bb50f6d539614cb1e5b4d.svg)

![](images/6a/6a294de4a5f2ff5755d8ceb5b91bb8920685a1cf2b5e727c5b5fdcfaaf0b89b0.svg)

I. $A$ is not invertible

II. $\textrm{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^4$

III. $\textrm{rank}(A)=4$

value:
Since $A$ is a $4 \times 4$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following: 

![](images/4b/4b42fd4ec8ccf491a1244a648af6fe40ce846fad388685e36d499783a095f8f7.svg)

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since 
![](images/32/327a582d15b82ebccda48358062310e6ad5c3bb2689f2024d76a8f8e7e1401a0.svg)
we conclude that 

$$
\textrm{dim(Null}(A))=1 \neq 0.
$$

So,  according to the invertible matrix theorem, the matrix $A$ is not invertible.

- Statement II is false. Since the matrix $A$ is not invertible, then by the invertible matrix theorem, we must have $\textrm{Col}(A) \neq \mathbb{R}^4.$

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is not invertible, then by the invertible matrix theorem, we must have $\textrm{rank}(A) \neq 4.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$A$ is invertible ![](images/dc/dc72aea1969143a926fd637d3360bb42116b27545a748923069f4ae732bd700f.svg)

$\qquad$ *If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\textrm{Null}(A) = \{\mathbf{ 0}\},$ then $\det(A) = 0.$* $\:{\color{red}\times}$

Since $\textrm{Null}(A) = \{\mathbf{ 0}\},$ then according to the invertible matrix theorem, the matrix $A$ must be invertible, which means $\det(A) \ne 0.$

- The following statement is true:

$\qquad$ *If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\textrm{Null}(A) = \{\mathbf{ 0}\},$ then $\textrm{rank}(A) = n.$* $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

- The following statement is true:

$\qquad$ *If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\textrm{Null}(A) = \{\mathbf{ 0}\},$ then $A$ has $n$ pivot columns.* $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$ 

Indeed, since $A$ is invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\textrm{dim(Col}(A))=n,$ which means that $A$ has exactly $n$ pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

The **pivots** of a matrix in row echelon form are the first non-zero entries in each row of the matrix.

For example, given the matrix 
![](images/ad/addf5cd1e1219a1e1ce28f3d27d1b000b3a99640ff89a62e55b66f3a5cdb3521.svg)
which is in row echelon form, let's find the pivots of $A.$

- The first non-zero entry in the first row is the entry $a_{11}=1.$ So this is a pivot.

- The first non-zero entry of the second row is $a_{22}=1.$ So this is also a pivot.

- The first non-zero entry in the third row is $a_{34}=1.$ Therefore this is a pivot.

The pivots of $A$ are highlighted below.

![](images/96/96dcf8cf9f0d387e0539ea04dd7ae4a498534361ad6bd5ed3bb119ae21f0416a.svg)

The **pivot columns** of a matrix in row echelon form are simply the columns in which the pivots appear.

For our matrix $A$, we can see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $4$th columns.

The non-pivot columns are the columns that do not contain a pivot. So for the matrix $A,$ the only non-pivot column is the $3$rd column.

Suppose that $A$ is a symmetric matrix. Then, we have the following properties:

- $-A$ is symmetric

- $A^m$ is symmetric for any positive integer $m$

- $A^{-1}$ is symmetric for nonsingular $A$

If $A$ and $B$ are $n\times n$ symmetric matrices, we have the following properties:

- $A+B$ is symmetric

- The product $A\cdot B$ is *not* always symmetric. For example, if 
![](images/e4/e41d28b6c6562ada530024fe6ab29cc16447dce14b2f741b8b35758618c78103.svg)
then the product $A\cdot B$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot B & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\,\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

 
which is *not* symmetric.

Finally, the following two properties can be used to construct symmetric matrices:

- $A + A^T$ is symmetric for any *square* matrix $A$

- $A^T A$ and $A A^T$ are symmetric for *any* matrix $A$

The last property is true for *any* $m\times n$ matrix. This property is particularly useful, as we'll discover in future lessons.

A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A = A^T
$$

Equivalently, $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the sum or difference between two symmetric matrices is symmetric.

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 
![](images/81/812e9888b920e0338fd72116464b8b96c8c272f95f180cd46aa3f1db9afac8d2.svg)
Their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

The dimension of the column space of a matrix $A$ is called the **rank of $A$**. It's usually denoted by $\textrm{rank}(A)$. So, 

$$
\textrm{rank}(A) = \textrm{dim}(\textrm{Col}(A)).
$$

For example, to find the rank of 
![](images/b9/b91bd53b8f1807be516e2477b37fbcd9c3a7415d6cf848d84aa085bc510b5eb4.svg)
we write $A$ in row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that there are $2$ pivot columns, namely, the $1$st and the $2$nd. This implies that the first and the second columns of $A$ form a basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)$ and, therefore, the dimension of $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is equal to $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}A(BC)=(AB)C\ne (BA)C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only statement I is true.

Suppose we want to solve the following system of linear equations using the elimination method:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=1 \\ x-y &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

As it stands, adding the two equations will not eliminate any of the variables. 

However, suppose we want to eliminate the variable $x$. We begin by multiplying the second equation by $\color{blue}-1$, which gives the following equivalent system:

![](images/72/724119f2404af61332fcabbb5cda3522f9d338a4c6427084e5901e1ca7cd4498.svg)

Then, we add the two resulting equations together. This will eliminate the variable $x,$ allowing us to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\cancel{x}+2y & =1 \\ -\cancel{x}+y & =2 \\ (2y+y) & =(1+2) \\ 3y & =3 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $y=1.$ However, we still need to find $x.$ To do this, we substitute $y=1$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x-y & =-2 \\ x-(1) & =-2 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-1$ and $y=1,$ which can be expressed as $(-1, 1).$

\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=1 \\ x-y &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

As it stands, adding the two equations will not eliminate any of the variables. 

However, suppose we want to eliminate the variable $x$. We begin by multiplying the second equation by $\color{blue}-1$, which gives the following equivalent system:

![](images/72/724119f2404af61332fcabbb5cda3522f9d338a4c6427084e5901e1ca7cd4498.svg)

Then, we add the two resulting equations together. This will eliminate the variable $x,$ allowing us to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\cancel{x}+2y & =1 \\ -\cancel{x}+y & =2 \\ (2y+y) & =(1+2) \\ 3y & =3 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $y=1.$ However, we still need to find $x.$ To do this, we substitute $y=1$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x-y & =-2 \\ x-(1) & =-2 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-1$ and $y=1,$ which can be expressed as $(-1, 1).$

Consider the following system of equations:

$$
{3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4
$$

To show that this system has infinitely many solutions, we solve the system using elimination.

Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-2$, then we get a $-6x$ term that can cancel with the $6x$ term in the second equation:

$$
{3x - y =-2 \mid \mid \cdot (-2); 6x - 2y =-4
$$

When we add the two equations, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-6x + 2y &= 4 \\
6x - 2y &= -4 \\
0 &= (4 - 4) \\
0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The statement $0=0$ is *always* true. This implies that this system of equations has *infinitely many solutions*.

Geometrically, this means that the equations

$$
{\color{red}3x - y =-2}
$$

and

$$
{\color{blue}6x -2y=-4}
$$

For example, if we multiply the equation of the first line by $2$, we get the second line!

$$

$$

When a system of equations has one solution, we can describe the solution as a single point $(x,y)$. This represents the point where the two lines intersect.

Now, suppose a system of equations has *infinitely many* solutions. Can we describe the solutions to the system in a similar way?

Indeed, we can. To demonstrate, consider the following system:

$$
{3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4
$$

Earlier, we showed that this system has infinitely many solutions. Therefore, the corresponding lines coincide.

Our goal is to express *all* the solutions of this system in the form $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$. To do this, we find the corresponding $y$-coordinate for each $x$-coordinate by solving one of the equations for $y$. It doesn't matter which, so let's pick the first equation.

$$
3x - y =-2⇒y = 3x + 2
$$

Therefore, for any given $x$-value, the corresponding $y$-value is

$$
y = 3x+2
$$

Finally, we can express the intersection points as

$$
({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}}) = \left({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{3x+2}}\right)
$$

where $\color{blue}x$ is *any* number.

The points of intersection of the lines correspond to the solutions of the following system:

$$
{3x + 2y = 2; 6x + 4y = 4
$$

We will solve the system using elimination. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-2$, then we will get a $-6x$ term that can cancel with the $6x$ term in the second equation:

$$
{3x + 2y = 2 \mid \mid \cdot (-2); 6x + 4y = 4
$$

When we add the two equations, it turns out that both variables cancel, and we obtain a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-6x - 4y &= -4 \\
6x + 4y &= 4 \\
0 &= (-4 + 4) \\
0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the lines have infinitely many intersection points.

We want to find an expression that represents every solution to the system. Any value of $x$ is a solution, and we can find the corresponding $y$-coordinate for each $x$-coordinate by solving one of the lines for $y$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x + 2y &= 2 \\
2y &= 2 - 3x \\
y &= \frac{2 - 3x}{2} \\
y &= 1 - \frac{3}{2}x
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points of intersection are

$$
\left(x,1-\dfrac{3}{2}x \right)
$$

where $x$ is any number.

Powers of matrices are similar to powers of numbers. If $A$ is a matrix, then $A^n$ is $A$ multiplied by itself $n$ times: 

$$
A^n = \underbrace{A\:\cdot\: A\:\cdot\: \ldots \:\cdot\: A}_{\Large{n\text{ times}}}
$$

For $A$ to be conformable with itself, $A$ needs to be a square matrix. So we can only take powers of square matrices.

To demonstrate, suppose that
![](images/81/81537bed0eafc982114b89fc84baeac44f7a75997c89df5a0f89b8b0a00b2da3.svg)

Then we can calculate $A^2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot 2 & 3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1 \\ 2\cdot 3+1\cdot 2 & 2\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 8 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

We say that $A^0 = I,$ the identity matrix of the same dimension as $A.$

Now that we know how to compute powers of matrices, we can evaluate polynomials where the input is a square matrix. 

For example, consider the polynomial

$$
f(X) = X^2 + 4X + 3.
$$

Note that, in order to evaluate this polynomial for an input matrix $X,$ we need to interpret any constants as multiples of the identity matrix. So, we interpret the polynomial as

$$
f(X) = X^2 + 4X + 3I.
$$

For example, if ![](images/6a/6abb7cbdef9c5d7b23d8519468b174de369cfe4af4b9f8c4578ce7dc74812f63.svg) then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and we can evaluate $f(A)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{2}+4A+3I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}+4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 & 4 \\ 0 & 8\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+4+3 & 3+4+0 \\ 0+0+0 & 4+8+3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 7 \\ 0 & 15\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

To take the **transpose of a matrix**, we interchange each of its columns with the corresponding row. That is, row $1$ becomes column $1,$ row $2$ becomes column $2,$ and so on. A superscript ${}^{T}$ is used to denote the transpose operation.

For example, the transpose of the $2 \times 3$ matrix ${X}$ is the following $3 \times 2$ matrix $X^T\mathbin{:}$

$$
{X} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		{\color{red}7} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}-4}  \\
        		{\color{blue}-3} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

        \qquad\implies\qquad

	{X}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		{\color{red}7} & {\color{blue}-3}  \\
        		{\color{red}2} & {\color{blue}1}  \\
        		{\color{red}-4} & {\color{blue}0}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

The first row of $X$ becomes the first column of $X^T,$ and the second row of $X$ becomes the second column of $X^T.$

Note that transposing a matrix swaps its dimensions. In general, we have the following property:

> *When a matrix is transposed, its dimensions switch from $m \times n$ to $n \times m.$*

Also, notice that the transpose of a column vector is a row vector:

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		5  \\
        		4  \\
                        2 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

       \qquad \implies\qquad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		5 & 4 & 2
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

Similarly, the transpose of a row vector is a column vector:

$$
{B} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		8 & -10 & 0 & 6
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

        \qquad\implies\qquad

	{B}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		8  \\
                        -10  \\
                        0  \\
                        6
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

Remember that transposing a matrix swaps the rows and columns. So, if $B=A^T,$ then $b_{ij}=a_{ji}$ for all values of $i$ and $j.$ 

Geometrically, when a matrix is transposed, the diagonal elements (those with $i=j$) remain the same while all other elements are reflected across the diagonal.  For example,

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \qquad  \implies\qquad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & 1  \\
        		\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack.
$$

Also,  transposing a matrix twice results in the original matrix. More precisely, for any matrix $A,$ we have

$$
\left( A^T\right)^T = A.
$$

This happens because, in the first transpose, we swap the rows of $A$ for the columns, and then in the second transpose, we swap them back again. For example,

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \quad  \implies\quad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & 1  \\
        		\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \quad  \implies\quad

	\left( {A}^T\right)^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack =A.
$$

Finally, for any numbers $c_1,c_2$ and any $m \times n$ matrices $A,B$ we have the following rule:

$$
(c_1 A \pm c_2 B)^T = c_1 A^T \pm c_2 B^T
$$

$$

To express $kA,$ we multiply each entry of $A$ by $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & 8 \\ 12 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2k & 6k & 8k \\ 12k & 0 & -4k\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the above result equal to the matrix given for $kA$ in the problem statement:

$$
\left\lbrack
    	\begin{matrix}
        	2k & 6k & 8k  \\
        	12k & 0 & -4k
    	\end{matrix}
    	\right\rbrack
=
\left\lbrack
    	\begin{matrix}
        	1 & 3 & 4  \\
        	6 & 0 & -2
    	\end{matrix}
    	\right\rbrack
$$

We can solve for $k$ by equating any two corresponding (nonzero) elements. Let's choose the top-left elements, $2k$ and $1.$ Equating these elements, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2k & =1 \\ k & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We would still get the same result if we chose any other two corresponding (nonzero) elements.
